title: Learning Behavior-oriented Knowledge Tracing

problem.claim: Online learning systems need to track how learners' knowledge states evolve to support downstream personalized services.

gap.claim: Existing methods primarily analyze responses as right or wrong and omit learning behaviors such as answering speed and number of attempts, despite their relevance to knowledge acquisition and response reliability.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes the Learning Behavior-oriented Knowledge Tracing model to explicitly model the effects of learning behaviors on learners' knowledge states.
The model separately estimates the quantitative effects of Speed, Attempts, and Hints, captures dependencies among multiple learning behaviors, and fuses their effects.
The model integrates forgetting with knowledge acquisition to update changing knowledge states.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that extensive experiments on several public datasets produce better performance prediction than existing methods.
The authors report that LBKT provides good interpretability for tracking learners' knowledge states by incorporating learning behavior effects.
The authors report that the code is publicly available.

narrative_sequence.summary: Tracking evolving learner knowledge states supports personalized services in online learning.
Existing approaches focus on correctness responses and omit informative learning behaviors.
LBKT models individual and dependent effects of learning behaviors and incorporates forgetting into knowledge-state updates.
Experiments on several public datasets are reported to improve performance prediction and interpretability over existing methods.

source_observation.claim: Learning behaviors such as speed, attempts, and hints are modeled alongside response correctness.

interpretation.claim: Behavioral process signals may provide information about latent learner state beyond outcome labels.

application.claim: Knowledge-tracing or learner-modeling systems could incorporate process features when available.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that these behavioral signals improve performance across settings beyond the reported public-dataset experiments.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, or magnitude of reported improvements.
The abstract does not detail the model architecture or the quantitative estimation procedure.
The abstract does not establish independent verification of the reported results.
